title: probe
text:
Before kavacha builds an app or opens a window, it needs a few facts about the machine it is on: whether a native window can be opened, which installed Python py2app can build with, whether the app’s local server has started, and whether a copy of the app is already running. This module finds them out. None of its functions raise when the answer is no. They return None, False or an empty list instead, so a caller can print a clear message.
pywebview is the library that draws the native window. It uses a different web engine on each platform and calls each one a GUI: cocoa on macOS, edgechromium (Microsoft Edge WebView2) on Windows and gtk on Linux. BACKENDS maps Python’s sys.platform names to these. FRAMEWORK_CANDIDATES is used by framework_python, further down.
backend looks up the GUI for a platform, the current one by default, and returns None for a platform pywebview does not support. shell_ready checks the two things a window needs, a supported platform and an installed pywebview, and returns (True, gui) or (False, reason). Call it before opening a window, so that a missing dependency produces a readable message instead of an import error.


source

shell_ready
def shell_ready(
    platform:NoneType=None
):
(ok, why): whether a native window can be opened here, and what is missing if not.




source

backend
def backend(
    platform:NoneType=None
):
pywebview’s GUI name for platform, or None where there is no supported webview.


The examples below look up three platforms, then check readiness for a platform with no backend and for macOS.

backend('darwin'), backend('linux'), backend('plan9')

('cocoa', 'gtk', None)



test_eq(shell_ready('plan9'), (False, 'no native webview backend for plan9'))
ok, why = shell_ready('darwin')
test_eq(ok, why == 'cocoa')

is_framework
def is_framework(
    python:NoneType=None
):
Whether python (default: this interpreter) is a macOS framework build py2app can use.




source

py_version
def py_version(
    python
):
The (major, minor) of python, or None when it will not say.


py2app copies the Python interpreter into the bundle, and it can only do that with a framework build. A framework build is the macOS layout that python.org, Homebrew and Apple’s command line tools install, with the interpreter inside a Python.framework folder. The interpreters uv and pyenv download are python-build-standalone builds, which are laid out differently and cannot be embedded.
is_framework checks one interpreter by running it and asking. With no argument it checks the Python running kavacha. When it checks another interpreter, it also requires Python 3.12 or later. py_version asks an interpreter for its (major, minor) version. framework_python goes through FRAMEWORK_CANDIDATES, the usual install paths, and returns the first framework build it finds, or None. All three treat an interpreter that is missing or will not run as a no, without raising.
The example uses three stand-in interpreters, small shell scripts that answer the probe the way a real one would. The first is a framework build of 3.13, which py2app can use. The second is a framework build of 3.11, which is too old. The third is a standalone 3.13, whose PYTHONFRAMEWORK setting is empty, as it is for every interpreter uv and pyenv install.

is_framework(fw), is_framework(old), is_framework(pbs)

(True, False, False)




source

wait_for_http
def wait_for_http(
    url, timeout:int=60, interval:float=0.1
):
Wait until url answers with a success status or timeout seconds pass, and return whether it did.


An app’s window should not load its page until the local server is listening, or the user sees a connection error. wait_for_http requests url every interval seconds until a request succeeds or timeout seconds pass, and returns True or False. Here the server has to answer with a success status, so a 404 counts as not ready. kavacha.window has its own wait_for_http, which accepts any HTTP response.

test_eq(wait_for_http(url), True)
test_eq(wait_for_http(url + 'missing', timeout=.3, interval=.05), False)



source

running_from
def running_from(
    bundle, ps_output:NoneType=None
):
PIDs of processes whose executable is inside bundle.


Rebuilding an app while a copy of it is running breaks the running copy, because the build replaces files it is still reading. running_from lists the process IDs of programs whose executable is inside the folder bundle. It reads the output of ps, or the text you pass as ps_output, which is how the example runs without a real app. Only the executable path counts, so a grep that mentions the bundle, or an app in a folder with a similar name, does not match. The current process is never listed, and if ps cannot run the result is an empty list.

ps = """  PID COMMAND
  101 /Apps/Demo.app/Contents/MacOS/Demo --serve
  102 /usr/bin/grep -r /Apps/Demo.app
  103 /Apps/Demo.app.old/Contents/MacOS/Demo
  104 /bin/zsh
"""
running_from('/Apps/Demo.app', ps)

[101]

title: lock
text:
A thin app gets its Python packages from a lock: a pinned project (pyproject.toml, uv.lock, .python-version) and a signed manifest.json. A new lock reaches people with no new app build. contract/api-1.md gives the formats; this module makes and checks locks, smoke-tests one as the launcher builds it, signs it with SSH keys, and publishes it on the app’s GitHub releases.
Everything app-specific comes from a Thin spec. An app adds its own checks in a hooks file (Thin.hooks): extra_reqs() gives each extra’s requirements, checks(s, base, port) runs against the first server, and smoke(s) runs more checks after it.

d = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(d/'pyproject.toml').write_text('p'); (d/'uv.lock').write_text('l'); (d/'.python-version').write_text('3.12.16\n')
test_eq(lock_hash(d, '0.13.6'), '2b6ad4d75869cd770d5cf35be37c47dc40fe7cfce61490729959b38333e9472a')

Whether a wheel filename installs on python and platform.

test_eq([wheel_fits(f) for f in ('a-1.0-cp313-cp313-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl', 'a-1.0-cp39-abi3-macosx_10_12_universal2.whl', 'a-1.0-cp312-cp312-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl')], [True, True, False])
test_eq(wheel_fits('a-1.0-cp313-cp313-win_amd64.whl', platform='win32-x64'), True)
test_eq(wheel_fits('a-1.0-cp313-cp313-manylinux_2_17_x86_64.whl', platform='linux-x64'), True)



The lock tool
Lock holds one app’s spec and the folders that follow from it. Its methods are the lock tool’s commands. Lock.hooks loads the app’s hooks file once.


source

Lock
def Lock(
    t:Thin, root:NoneType=None
):
The lock tool for one thin app.


The pinned uv is the one the app ships: <PREFIX>UV, else the app’s build folder. A uv of another version is refused, so a lock is never made or tested with a uv the app does not have.


The child environment
child_env is what the launcher’s own uv runs get, and server_env is what the server gets: the person’s environment, less the dropped names, with the tool folders on PATH. server_env_old is what launcher 1.0.0 gave its server; a newer lock must still run under it.

lk = Lock(Thin('Demo', repo='me/demo'), d)
e = lk.child_env(dict(PATH='/usr/bin', VIRTUAL_ENV='/v', UV_INDEX_URL='x', DEMO_HOST_TOKEN='t'), cache='/c', python='/py', python_version='3.13.18', env='/e')
test_eq(('VIRTUAL_ENV' in e, 'UV_INDEX_URL' in e, 'DEMO_HOST_TOKEN' in e, e['UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT']), (False, False, False, '/e'))
test_eq(lk.sync_args('/l', ['a'], inexact=True)[-3:], ['--inexact', '--extra', 'a'])



Writing the pinned project
pyproject writes the pinned project for app version v. The app’s package comes from a wheel URL on its GitHub release (or a local wheel, for a lock that cannot be published). The cooldown is exclude-newer, Thin.cooldown days before the lock; the owner’s packages are exempt. A pinned wheel (Thin.wheels) comes by URL.

lk = Lock(Thin('Demo', repo='me/demo', extras=['x'], wheels={'big': dict(version='1', url='https://w/big-1-py3-none-any.whl', sha256='00')}), tempfile.mkdtemp())
p = tomllib.loads(lk.pyproject('1.0', 'https://w/demo.whl', {'x': ['big==1']}, ['mine'], datetime(2026, 11, 6, tzinfo=timezone.utc)))
test_eq((p['project']['dependencies'], p['tool']['uv']['exclude-newer'], p['tool']['uv']['sources']['big']), (['demo==1.0'], '2026-10-30T00:00:00Z', {'url': 'https://w/big-1-py3-none-any.whl'}))



Checking a lock
check refuses a lock the app cannot install: another index, an editable, git or path source, a package with no fitting wheel, a pinned wheel in the base env or with another hash, and no required environment. It gives every reason, so one run lists them all.

packages

make writes the pinned project, locks it twice with the pinned uv (the second time with each extra pinned == to what the first chose), checks it, and prints its hash. UV_NO_CONFIG=1 drops the settings in [tool.uv], so the cooldown goes on the command line too.


source

cooldown_args
def cooldown_args(
    d
):
The pinned project’s cooldown as uv flags, which UV_NO_CONFIG does not drop.




The manifest
manifest is what the launcher checks before it installs a lock. The app’s own version is under the key of its package name, such as leela.


Signing
The keys are SSH Ed25519 keys in ~/.ssh, named by Thin.key_names: main and emergency. Signing is SSHSIG with the namespace Thin.sig_ns, through the SSH agent when it holds the key. The tools check a signature with ssh-keygen -Y verify; the launcher checks SSHSIG itself.


Fixtures and dev locks
fixtures writes SSHSIG fixtures with throwaway keys, under a temporary HOME, so no real key or agent is ever used. dev_lock signs a lock with a throwaway key, for a local app build that is not for release.


source

fixtures
def fixtures(
    out, ns:str='app-lock', platform:str='darwin-arm64'
):
SSHSIG fixtures made by ssh-keygen with throwaway keys under a temporary HOME.



f = fixtures(Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()))
lk = Lock(Thin('App'), d)
test_eq(lk.verify_sig(f/'message.json', f/'main.sig', f/'keys.pub'), True)
test_eq([lk.verify_sig(f/'message.json', f/f'{k}.sig', f/'keys.pub') for k in ('emergency', 'stranger', 'wrongns')], [True, False, False])



The smoke test
lock_test builds the env as the launcher does, in a temp folder, with the same uv, child environment and command. Then smoke checks it, and a pass writes a test record for this lock hash. Smoke is what a hook gets: the env, the temp folders, and step, serve and the HTTP helpers.

    token

The launcher’s control server, enough for a smoke test: every question gets Yes.

live_ports

    name, home:NoneType=None
):
The ports of the app the person runs, from its real serving.json: no test may call them.


Smoke.get and Smoke.post never reach the app the person runs: a port in its serving.json is refused. Proxies are never used.


source

Smoke
def Smoke(
    lk, env_dir, results, extras:tuple=(), wait:int=180
):
What a smoke check needs: the env, temp folders, results, and the helpers to start and call a server.


Smoke.serve starts the server from an env as the launcher does: the host variables in its environment, the token as one stdin line, never in argv, the environment, a file or a log. It waits for the health route, runs checks(base, port), then stops it. A server must stop within 5 s of SIGTERM, with the streams the app’s hold_open(s, base, port) hook names held open, as a window holds them.
Lock.smoke runs the steps every thin app needs, then the app’s hooks: uv pip check, the imports, the first server with the app’s checks, then the app’s smoke(s), then each extra’s check (extra_check(x) gives Python arguments, else import x).


The env from a copy
The launcher builds a new lock’s env from an APFS clone of the env in use. seed does the same here: a clone with the old path rewritten in bin/ and pyvenv.cfg, and no bytecode. incremental then adds one extra with uv sync and checks that the copy installs only that, works, and names only itself.

b as a clone of env a, with a’s path rewritten in bin/ and pyvenv.cfg, and no bytecode.

The channel
Each lock is a release lock-<n>; the release lock-channel holds the signed pointers channel.json and channel-test.json. A pointer names its channel, so a test pointer served as stable is refused. gh runs with the keyring’s sign-in, never a GITHUB_TOKEN from the environment.

    n, manifest_sha, name, at:NoneType=None
):
A channel pointer; it names its channel.




source

fetch
def fetch(
    url, dst:NoneType=None
):
The bytes at url, also written to dst.


refusals is every reason publish refuses: no public keys, no signing key, a failed check, a tree that is not clean and pushed, no fresh passing record from this uv and this test code, and a lower app version than the last lock (unless allow_downgrade).
publish signs the lock as lock-<n>, checks what GitHub serves, then points the test channel at it. promote copies the test pointer to stable. verify checks a channel as the app does.
diff lists what changed against the published lock. An owner package version with no git tag in Thin.owner_org is flagged. wheel builds the app’s wheel from a tag in a clean worktree, and attaches it to that release.


Checking a built app
verify_app checks a built bundle without opening it: the plist, the launcher, the pinned uv, the bootstrap lock and its signature, the generated files, and the size gates of the spec. A bundle whose keys are not the committed keys is signed with a throwaway key, and it says so.


The command line
kavacha lock <command> runs in the app’s folder (or --root). Each command is one method above.

title: icons
text:
An app needs its icon in several formats: an .icns file for a macOS bundle, an .ico file for Windows, and a small PNG favicon for the web page in the window. This module makes all of them from one square image. It needs Pillow, which the icons extra installs. Most callers only need icons_for, at the end of the page.
An .icns file is built from a folder of PNG files with fixed names, which macOS’s iconutil tool reads. ICNS_SIZES lists the ten names and the pixel size of each. The @2x names are double-size copies for Retina screens, so some sizes appear twice and there are seven distinct sizes. ICO_SIZES are the sizes ico puts in a Windows icon by default.

ICNS_SIZES[:4]

((16, 'icon_16x16'),
 (32, 'icon_16x16@2x'),
 (32, 'icon_32x32'),
 (64, 'icon_32x32@2x'))


_open loads the source image as RGBA and checks it. An app icon has to be square and at least 512 pixels wide. macOS draws icons at up to 1024 pixels, and a smaller source would be scaled up and look blurred, so it is refused instead. Any format Pillow can read works; the example opens a JPEG.

_open(root/'logo.jpg').mode, _open(root/'logo.jpg').size

('RGBA', (1024, 1024))


These are the two errors you get for a source that is not square or is too small. The examples work in a temporary folder, shown here as /proj.

Image.new('RGBA', (800, 400)).save(root/'wide.png')
for p in ('wide.png', 'small.png'):
    try: _open(root/p)
    except ValueError as e: print(str(e).replace(str(root), '/proj'))

/proj/wide.png is 800x400; an app icon has to be square
/proj/small.png is 128px; macOS draws icons at 1024 and will upscale this

def icns(
    src, out, keep_iconset:bool=False
):
Build the .icns file out from src with macOS iconutil.




source

iconset
def iconset(
    src, out

The .iconset folder iconutil turns into an .icns. Returns the folder.


iconset writes the ten PNG files into the folder out and returns it. icns builds the .icns file out from them with iconutil, then deletes the PNG folder unless keep_iconset is set. iconutil only exists on macOS, so elsewhere icns raises a RuntimeError, as the second example shows. The folder is deleted either way.

out = iconset(logo, root/'Set.iconset')
sorted((Image.open(p).size[0], p.stem) for p in out.glob('*.png'))

[(16, 'icon_16x16'),
 (32, 'icon_16x16@2x'),
 (32, 'icon_32x32'),
 (64, 'icon_32x32@2x'),

 (256, 'icon_128x128@2x'),

 (1024, 'icon_512x512@2x')]



try: print(icns(logo, root/'Demo.icns').name)
except RuntimeError as e: print(e)

def ico(
    src, out, sizes:tuple=(16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 128, 256)

A Windows .ico from one square image. Pillow writes every size into the one file.


ico writes one Windows .ico file that holds the image at each size in sizes. A size above 256 pixels, the largest an .ico can hold, is left out, which is why the second example asks for 512 and gets only 16 and 32.

with Image.open(ico(logo, root/'assets'/'Demo.ico')) as im: print(sorted(im.info['sizes']))
with Image.open(ico(logo, root/'small.ico', sizes=(16, 32, 512))) as im: print(sorted(im.info['sizes']))

title: host
text:
A thin app’s launcher starts the server with <PREFIX>HOST_URL in its environment and the token as one line on stdin (contract/api-1.md). This module is what the server does with them. HostClient holds the control server’s address and token, and asks the launcher what only it can do: a native question, a one-time grant, an update, an extra. It needs only the standard library and fastcore, so the server imports it with no window code.

The names the launcher owns
owned lists what the launcher sets for its child. No login shell and no stored value may replace these, or the names in STEER, which would move the server off the env the launcher built. host_env is the environment block the launcher adds; the lock tests use it to start a server as the launcher does.


source

host_env
def host_env(
    prefix, url, version:str='0.0.0-test', bundle:str='', n:int=0, hash:str='', uv:str=''
):
The variables the launcher gives its server; never the token, which goes on stdin.




source

owned
def owned(
    prefix
):



test_eq(owned('LEELA_')[:2], ('LEELA_HOST_URL', 'LEELA_HOST_TOKEN'))
test_eq('LEELA_HOST_TOKEN' in host_env('LEELA_', 'http://127.0.0.1:9'), False)



The client
HostClient.take is the first thing a server does in host mode. It reads the token line, keeps it in memory, and puts stdin on /dev/null, so no child can read the token. A token in the environment is ignored with a warning. No line, an empty line or a late line stops the server.


source

HostClient
def HostClient(
    prefix, app:str='the app', data:str=''
):
The server’s side of the launcher’s control server: its address, its token, and the names under prefix.




source

HostError
def HostError(
    *args, **kwargs
):
The launcher did not answer, or refused.



r, w = os.pipe(); os.write(w, b'tok\nrest'); os.close(w)
h, e = HostClient('DEMO_', 'Demo'), {'DEMO_HOST_URL': 'http://127.0.0.1:9', 'DEMO_HOST_TOKEN': 'x'}
test_eq((h.take(e, fd=r, timeout=1), h.state['token'], e), (True, 'tok', {}))
test_eq(os.read(r, 4), b'')
os.close(r)

call makes one request to the launcher. It goes only to an http URL on 127.0.0.1 with a port, never through a proxy. Connecting fails fast; the answer may wait for a person.

h = HostClient('DEMO_'); h.state['url'] = 'http://example.com:80'
test_fail(lambda: h.call('/status'), contains='not a loopback')

The control routes a server calls by name. grant_ok asks whether the launcher issued a one-time nonce for a path; that is how a Finder open or a picked folder is trusted, with no token in the server’s hands. ask is a native question; any failure raises HostError, so a broken answer is never a No.

h = HostClient('DEMO_')
test_eq((h.grant_ok('n', '/x'), h.status()), (False, {}))
test_eq(h.health('1.2')['status'], 'ok')



A clean environment for the server’s children
Launcher 1.0.0 gave its server uv’s build settings, PYTHONNOUSERSITE, NO_COLOR, VIRTUAL_ENV and the env’s bin on PATH. Every kernel, terminal and project uv run inherits the server’s environment, so scrub takes these out first. A newer lock still runs under the old launcher.


source

scrub
def scrub(
    env:NoneType=None, prefix:NoneType=None
):
Take out uv’s build settings, PYTHONNOUSERSITE, NO_COLOR=1, a VIRTUAL_ENV that is this env, and this env’s bin on PATH.



e = scrub(dict(UV_X='1', PYTHONNOUSERSITE='1', NO_COLOR='1', VIRTUAL_ENV='/e', PATH='/e/bin:/usr/bin'), prefix='/e')
test_eq(e, dict(PATH='/usr/bin'))



The app’s tools on an agent’s PATH
An agent’s shell runs the console scripts of some packages in the app’s env by name. link_tools links them into bin beside the launcher’s envs/, so an env switch changes them. On Windows a link needs rights a person may not have, so each tool is a .cmd shim.


source

link_tools
def link_tools(
    names, src:NoneType=None, dst:NoneType=None, windows:NoneType=None
):
Link names from the scripts folder src into dst, and remove what an earlier env left there. The folder.




source

agent_scripts
def agent_scripts(
    pkgs
):
The console scripts of pkgs in this env; never a python, pip or uv.



import tempfile
s, d = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()), Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(s/'kosha').write_text(''); (s/'kosha.exe').write_text(''); (d/'old.cmd').write_text('')
link_tools(['kosha', 'none'], s, d, windows=True)
test_eq(sorted(p.name for p in d.iterdir()), ['kosha.cmd'])
d2 = link_tools(['kosha'], s, Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()), windows=False)
test_eq((d2/'kosha').is_symlink(), True)
test_eq(HostClient('X_', 'Demo').tools_dir('/a/envs/0123'), Path('/a/bin'))

title: ship
text:
A thin Mac app is kavacha’s launcher, the pinned uv, a signed bootstrap lock and three generated files, in one bundle. This module puts them together, signs the helper and then the app, notarizes and staples it, zips it, uploads it to the release app-v<V> and writes the Homebrew cask. The launcher is a kavacha release (Thin.launcher, checked against Thin.launcher_sha256), or a local build of swift/ for a test.

The pieces
fetch_uv downloads the pinned uv and checks it against the pinned sha256 before it unpacks it.


source

launcher
def launcher(
    t, out, local:NoneType=None
):
The launcher binary: local, else the kavacha release t.launcher, checked against t.launcher_sha256.




source

fetch_uv
def fetch_uv(
    lk, out:NoneType=None
):
The pinned uv in the app’s build folder, downloaded and checked when it is not there. Its path.




The bundle
bundle lays out the app as contract/api-1.md names it. An app’s plist() hook adds to the Info.plist, such as document types the app computes. It moves an old bundle aside, never into the trash of the person’s Mac.


source

bundle
def bundle(
    lk, out, exe, uv, lock, keys, icon:NoneType=None

title: kavacha
text:
kavacha (कवच, “armour”) is for Python web apps that run on the user’s own machine, such as a FastHTML app that uvicorn serves on 127.0.0.1. It does two jobs. While the app runs, it opens a native desktop window that shows the app, so the user gets an application with its own Dock icon and menu bar instead of a browser tab. At build time, it turns the project into a standalone application that carries its own copy of Python, so the user does not have to install Python to run it.
The build side relies on a freezer. A freezer is a tool that collects a Python program, the interpreter and every module the program imports into one folder that runs by itself. kavacha uses py2app on macOS, where that folder is a .app bundle, and py2exe on Windows. Each freezer has to be told about imports it cannot find by reading the code, and each leaves problems behind in the bundle it writes. kavacha keeps the description of your app in one place, turns it into the options each freezer expects, and repairs the bundle afterwards.

text:
Describe the app
An App describes the application once, and both freezers take their options from it.
from kavacha import App, tree, doc_types, mypyc_modules

app = App(
    name='Demo',
    entry='demo_app.py',
    version='1.2.3',
    icon='assets/Demo.icns',
    packages=['demo', 'fasthtml', 'uvicorn', 'numpy'],
    includes=['demo.cli', *mypyc_modules()],
    grafted=['apsw', 'playwright'],
    data=tree('demo/static', 'demo/static'),
    extras=['desktop'],
    doc_types=doc_types(['.py', '.rs', '.md']),
)
app.py2app_options()
entry is the script the app runs. packages are copied into the bundle whole. includes names single modules the freezer would miss because no import statement names them, such as the compiled helper modules mypyc_modules finds. grafted names packages that do not work from inside the freezer’s zip archive, so kavacha copies them in after the freezer has run. data lists files the app reads that are not Python, and tree builds that list from a folder. doc_types declares which files Finder may open with the app. extras are the optional dependency groups of your project that the build environment installs. py2app_options() and py2exe_options() return the options for each freezer. The spec page covers every field.

Build
from kavacha import build, check

check(app, root)
build(app, root, setup_py='packaging/macos/setup.py')
check reports what a build would do on this machine without changing anything: which freezer it would use, whether the Python it runs on can be used, whether pywebview is installed, and whether a copy of the app is running. build then does the work. root is your project folder and setup_py is the script that calls the freezer.
On macOS, py2app can only embed a framework build of Python, the kind python.org and Homebrew install. The interpreters uv and pyenv download are not framework builds. When the current Python is not one, build finds one, creates a virtual environment from it with the package versions pinned in uv.lock, and runs your build script again inside it. It refuses to overwrite an app that is running unless you pass force=True, and it writes the git commit the app was built from into the bundle. The build page has the details.

text:
A freezer’s output does not always run as it is, and it is often larger than it needs to be. This module fixes a bundle after the freezer has written it. Most of the work is for macOS, where py2app leaves more to fix. finish, near the end of the page, runs the repairs in order and is the function most callers need. The steps are also available one by one, so each can be run and tested on its own. sign comes last, after finish.

graft
def graft(
    app, name, python:NoneType=None
):
Copy the installed package name into a built bundle, replacing the freezer’s copy, and return where it went.


py2app puts pure Python modules into a zip archive inside the bundle, pythonXY.zip, and Python imports them from there. Some packages do not work from a zip: they read their own files from disk, or they carry native programs and libraries that must exist as real files. Copying such a package into the bundle after the freezer has run is called grafting.
graft copies the installed package name from the environment kavacha runs in into the bundle’s lib/pythonX.Y folder, deletes whatever the freezer left in its place, and returns where it put the package, relative to the bundle. It stops with an error if the package is not installed or if the bundle was built for a different Python version than python, which defaults to the running one.
It also compiles the copied files to bytecode in unchecked-hash mode. Python loads such .pyc files without comparing them to the source. A signed bundle is read-only, and without these files Python would try to write bytecode into it the first time the package is imported.

app, lib = mkapp('Demo.app')
(lib/'json.cpython-311-x86_64-linux-gnu.so').write_text('what the freezer flattened')
graft(app, 'json')

def is_macho(
    p

Whether p starts with a Mach-O or universal header.


Compiled programs and libraries on macOS are Mach-O files. A Mach-O file begins with load commands, a header that lists its segments, its code signature, its install name (the path other programs use to find it), its version, a UUID and the libraries it depends on. A universal file holds one Mach-O slice per CPU architecture.
is_macho checks whether a file starts with a Mach-O header. macho reads the header of each slice and returns those facts as a list of dicts, or None for a file that is not Mach-O. corrupt reports a file whose header does not describe its body, for example one whose last segment does not end where the file does. codesign refuses to sign such a file and reports “main executable failed strict validation”. The example reads the system’s own /usr/lib/dyld when it exists, which is the case on a Mac.

def mend_frameworks(
    app, search:tuple=()
):
Replace each corrupt library in Contents/Frameworks with a healthy installed copy, and report file names with more than one build installed.


py2app copies the native libraries a bundle needs into Contents/Frameworks and names each copy by its file name alone. When two different libraries share a file name, for example two builds of the same library shipped by two packages, the copies get mixed up: one file ends up with the body of one library and the header of the other, which makes it corrupt in the sense above.
mend_frameworks finds each corrupt file in Contents/Frameworks and replaces it with a healthy installed copy. It looks among the libraries the interpreter and the bundled packages link to, plus any folders in search, and prefers a copy the same size as the corrupt file, then the highest version. It then points the copy’s install name and dependencies at Contents/Frameworks and signs it ad hoc.
It returns two dicts. mended maps each repaired file name to the copy used, or to None when no healthy copy was found. clashes lists every file name that has more than one distinct build installed on this machine, whether or not it caused a problem this time. The example bundle has no Frameworks folder, so both are empty.

sign
def sign(
    app, identity, entitlements:NoneType=None, run:NoneType=None, waits:tuple=(5, 15, 30)
):
Code-sign every Mach-O file deepest first, then each framework, then the bundle, signing hardlinked files once and never using --deep.


macOS only runs a downloaded app if it is signed, and the signature has to cover every program and library inside it. sign signs the bundle with identity, the name of your signing certificate, or - for an ad hoc signature that only works on your own machine. It signs each Mach-O file first, deepest in the folder tree first, then each .framework, then the bundle, and finally verifies the result. It does not use codesign --deep, which would sign everything with the same options. Every file is signed with the hardened runtime (--options runtime), which Apple’s notarisation requires.
Executables get the entitlements file, as the bundle does. Libraries ending in .so or .dylib do not. Files that are hardlinks of one another are signed once: codesign --force writes a new file, which breaks the link, so sign links the other paths back to the signed file.
run is the function that runs each command. It is called as subprocess.run is called, so it must accept keyword arguments: each signing call passes stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True so that sign can read the error. The example passes one that records the commands instead of running them, so it needs no certificate.

app7 = root/'Sign.app'
for rel in ('Contents/MacOS/Sign', 'Contents/Resources/lib/a/node', 'Contents/Resources/lib/x.so'):
    (p := app7/rel).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True); p.write_bytes(b'\xcf\xfa\xed\xfe' + bytes(28))
(app7/'Contents/Resources/lib/a/node').chmod(0o755)
os.link(app7/'Contents/Resources/lib/a/node', app7/'Contents/Resources/lib/b')
calls = []
sign(app7, 'ID', 'ent.plist', run=lambda *a, **kw: calls.append([str(x) for x in a]))
[c[-1].replace(str(root), '') for c in calls]

Apple’s timestamp server sometimes does not answer. codesign then fails with “A timestamp was expected but was not found” or “The timestamp service is not available”, and a second try a little later works. sign tries such a file again after each wait in waits (5, 15 and 30 seconds) and prints one line per try. When the last try fails too, it raises that error. Any other codesign failure raises at once.
The fake runner below fails the first n signing calls with msg. It runs no program. With no waits, two timestamp failures come before one good signature:

def flaky(n, msg):
    "A fake `run` that fails the first `n` signing calls with `msg` on stderr, and records every call."
    calls = []
    def run(*a, **kw):
        calls.append([str(x) for x in a])
        if '--sign' in a and len(calls) <= n: raise subprocess.CalledProcessError(1, a, stderr=msg)
    return run, calls

run, calls = flaky(2, 'Sign.app/node: A timestamp was expected but was not found.')
sign(app7, 'ID', 'ent.plist', run=run, waits=(0, 0, 0))
test_eq(len(calls), 6)
test_eq(calls[0], calls[2])

A server that never answers fails after three retries, four tries in all. A failure that is not about the timestamp raises on the first try:

run, calls = flaky(99, 'The timestamp service is not available.')
test_fail(lambda: sign(app7, 'ID', run=run, waits=(0, 0, 0)), contains='returned non-zero')
test_eq(len(calls), 4)

run, calls = flaky(99, 'errSecInternalComponent')
test_fail(lambda: sign(app7, 'ID', run=run, waits=(0, 0, 0)), contains='returned non-zero')
test_eq(len(calls), 1)

def ShellApi(
    *args, **kwargs
):
What the page may ask the native window for, as window.pywebview.api.*.
The page in the window sometimes needs the operating system, for example to show the native folder chooser. pywebview allows this through a JavaScript API: the methods of a Python object become functions the page calls as window.pywebview.api.<method>(). ShellApi is that object.
pick_folder shows the platform’s folder chooser and returns the chosen path, or None if the user cancels. pick_path does the same with a chooser that takes a file or a folder, as File > Open does in a Mac app. open_folder and recent pass the request to the host’s on_open_folder and on_recent callbacks, which run_shell sets. Without a callback, open_folder returns False and recent returns an empty list. open_path takes either kind: a folder goes the way of open_folder, and a file goes to on_open_file, the callback a file opened from Finder reaches. A host that must tell a request from the page apart from a Finder or Dock open sets on_page_folder: open_folder then calls it in place of on_open_folder. on_picked gets each folder the person chooses in pick_folder or pick_path, before the page sees it, so the host can trust that one path. It is not called for a file or when the person cancels. pywebview calls these methods on its own worker threads, so the callbacks must be safe to call from any thread. dropped is for files dropped on the window, described with arm_drops below. The page cannot call the on_ callbacks themselves: pywebview offers the page every function an object lists, so ShellApi lists none of them.
set_background is for a page with themes. It takes the page’s background as #rrggbb and paints every open window’s native background with it, which is what shows while the window opens or grows faster than the page redraws. It also keeps the colour in background, so a window opened later starts on it. The colour is per app, not per window: pywebview does not say which window called. Anything that is not #rrggbb returns False and changes nothing.

quit_cleanly
def quit_cleanly(
    timeout:int=15, run_exit:NoneType=None, grace:float=1.0
):
Stop this process’s multiprocessing children, then run its atexit handlers, which a Cocoa quit’s C exit() skips.
When a Cocoa app quits, it ends the process with C’s exit(), which skips Python’s atexit handlers, and worker processes can outlive it. A worker pool started by forking, as fastcore.parallel does on macOS, keeps pipes open that hold its children alive. quit_cleanly terminates each child process of this one, kills any still running after one shared grace of a second, then runs the atexit handlers on a thread and waits at most timeout seconds for them. It reaps once more afterwards, for a pool a still-running thread started meanwhile, and returns the number of children it stopped. It sets quitting first, so a host’s background job can tell being reaped from failing. run_exit replaces the atexit handlers, which is how the test below checks it without exiting.
quit_on_sigterm makes a SIGTERM, the signal kill sends by default, quit the app the way Cmd+Q does, so that the same clean-up runs. It works on macOS only, must be called on the main thread, and is called by run_shell. A forked child gets the default SIGTERM back and lets go of the wakeup socket, and a multiprocessing child exits once its parent is gone, so a Force Quit or a crash leaves no idle worker behind. Once a quit begins, a second SIGTERM kills.

import os, signal, sys, time, multiprocessing as mp
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
from kavacha.window import quit_on_sigterm, quit_cleanly
def ignore(): signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, signal.SIG_IGN); time.sleep(60)
def nested(path):
    ex = ProcessPoolExecutor(2, mp_context=mp.get_context('fork')); list(ex.map(abs, range(4)))
    open(path, 'w').write(' '.join(str(p.pid) for p in mp.active_children())); time.sleep(60)
def alive(pid):
    try: os.kill(pid, 0); return True
    except OSError: return False
if __name__ == '__main__':
    r, w = quit_on_sigterm(); r.setblocking(False)
    fork = mp.get_context('fork')
    kid = fork.Process(target=time.sleep, args=(60,)); kid.start(); time.sleep(.3)
    kid.terminate(); kid.join(5)
    assert kid.exitcode == -signal.SIGTERM, kid.exitcode
    try: assert not r.recv(64), "a child's SIGTERM reached the parent's wakeup socket"
    except BlockingIOError: pass
    ex = ProcessPoolExecutor(4, mp_context=fork); list(ex.map(abs, range(8)))
    pool = [p.pid for p in mp.active_children()]
    stubborn = [fork.Process(target=ignore) for _ in range(4)]
    for p in stubborn: p.start()
    time.sleep(.5); t0 = time.time()
    assert quit_cleanly(run_exit=lambda: None, grace=.5) == 8
    assert time.time() - t0 < 4, f'{time.time()-t0:.1f}s: one shared grace, not one per child'
    assert not [p for p in pool if alive(p)], 'pool workers outlived quit_cleanly'
    assert signal.getsignal(signal.SIGTERM) == signal.SIG_DFL, 'a second SIGTERM must kill a hung quit'
    mid = fork.Process(target=nested, args=(sys.argv[1],)); mid.start()
    while not os.path.exists(sys.argv[1]) or not open(sys.argv[1]).read(): time.sleep(.1)
    grand = [int(x) for x in open(sys.argv[1]).read().split()]
    os.kill(mid.pid, signal.SIGKILL); mid.join()
    end = time.time() + 5
    while [g for g in grand if alive(g)] and time.time() < end: time.sleep(.2)
    assert not [g for g in grand if alive(g)], 'workers outlived a parent that was SIGKILLed'
    print('ok')
'''
if sys.platform == 'darwin':
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:

def watch_open_events(
    on_folder:NoneType=None, on_file:NoneType=None

Answer the odoc Apple Event Finder sends a running app. macOS only, best-effort.


When the user drops a folder on the app’s Dock icon, or opens a folder with the app from Finder, macOS sends the running app an “open documents” Apple Event, odoc. watch_open_events registers a handler for it that hands the paths in the event to open_paths, which calls on_folder for each folder and on_file for each file. run_shell registers it with the host’s callbacks, already wrapped by off_main_thread. The app delegate receives the same opens through application:openFiles:, and open_paths keeps a path that arrives both ways from being delivered twice. It returns the handler, or None on other platforms or if registration fails.
AppKit can only call methods on Objective-C objects, so the Dock menu rows and the Apple Event handler each need a small NSObject subclass that passes the call on to a Python function: RecentTarget for a Dock menu row and OpenHandler for the event. Where pyobjc is not installed, both classes are None, and the functions that use them only run on macOS.
A menu bar shows keyboard shortcuts next to its items, and pressing one runs the item even while the web page has focus. kavacha writes a shortcut as a chord, such as mod+s: modifier names joined by +, then a key, where mod means Cmd on a Mac. AppKit wants the same shortcut as a key equivalent, which is a single character, plus a modifier mask, a number with one bit per modifier key. CMD, CTRL, ALT and SHIFT are those bits, defined here so that chords can be parsed and tested on any platform.

(keyEquivalent, modifierMask) for one chord, or None when AppKit cannot spell it.


mac_key converts one chord to a (key, mask) pair. It accepts the modifiers mod, cmd, ctrl, alt, opt and shift, an upper-case letter as shorthand for shift and that letter, and named keys such as up, enter, tab and escape. For a sequence of chords, such as mod+k mod+s, it uses only the first.
AppKit matches a key equivalent against the character the key types, so Shift is written into the key and not into the mask: mod+shift+o is O with Command, and mod+shift+/ is ? with Command, the character Shift gives on a US keyboard. A named key such as an arrow types no character, so it keeps the Shift bit. mac_key returns None for hyper, which a window manager takes, and for a chord AppKit cannot show as a key equivalent, such as one with a function key or an unknown modifier like meta.

def menu_chord(

The AppKit chord for action: its first chord with a modifier, not reserved, from a global binding or the only scope with that chord.


A menu shortcut takes the key press before the web page sees it, so only some of the host’s bindings should become one. The host’s keymap is reached through lookup, a function that takes an action name and returns a Binding from kavacha.menus, or None. menu_chord looks up action and returns the AppKit chord of the binding’s first chord that uses a modifier other than shift and is not in RESERVED, and only when the binding either applies everywhere (its scope is global) or is the only binding of that chord in any scope (shared is false). A bare key such as /, or an editor chord that another pane uses too, stays with the page. A lookup that returns some other object with no shared attribute gets chords for its global bindings only.

A menu bar holding the rows of main, where a row fires only for its own chord.

title: spec
text:
A freezer needs to be told what goes into an app: the script to run, the packages to copy, the modules it would miss, the data files, the icon, and the metadata macOS reads from the bundle’s Info.plist. py2app and py2exe each take this as a dictionary of options, and they name the options differently. This module lets you write the description once, as an App, and produces either dictionary from it.


source

mypyc_modules
def mypyc_modules(
    site:NoneType=None
):
List the mypyc helper modules in site, which a freezer cannot find by following imports.




source

tree
def tree(
    src, dest, skip:tuple=()
):
List every file under src as the (dest_dir, [files]) pairs a freezer takes, with src mapped to dest.


Data files are files the app reads at run time that are not Python code, such as CSS, JavaScript and images. A freezer takes them as a list of (dest_dir, [files]) pairs, where dest_dir is a folder inside the bundle and files are paths on your disk. tree builds that list for a whole folder. It walks src, mirrors its layout under dest, skips hidden files, __pycache__ and any folder named in skip, and sorts the pairs so that two builds produce the same list. Pass the result as App(data=...). The example skips node_modules and the hidden .DS_Store.

data = tree(src, 'demo/static', skip=['node_modules'])
[(dest, [Path(f).name for f in files]) for dest, files in data]

[('demo/static', ['app.css']),
 ('demo/static/img', ['logo.png']),
 ('demo/static/js', ['app.js'])]


Some packages ship parts compiled with mypyc, and the compiled parts load a helper extension module whose file name contains __mypyc. Nothing imports that helper by name, so a freezer that follows import statements leaves it out and the app fails when it starts. mypyc_modules lists these helpers in the site-packages of the environment you build from, or in the folder site. Add the result to App(includes=...). The helpers’ file names include the Python version and platform, which is why they are looked up at build time instead of written into the spec by hand.

site = Path(tmp.name)/'site'; site.mkdir()
for f in ('chardet__mypyc.cpython-313-darwin.so', 'numpy.cpython-313-darwin.so'): (site/f).write_text('')
mypyc_modules(site)

['chardet__mypyc']


A freezer also pulls in modules no app needs, because something in the environment mentions them. DEFAULT_EXCLUDES lists the usual ones: build tools such as setuptools and the freezers themselves, the standard library’s test suite, other GUI toolkits, and matplotlib. GUI_MODULE names pywebview’s module for each platform, so that a build can leave out the two it does not use.

App
def App(
    name:str, entry:str, version:str='0.0.0', build:str='', icon:str='', modern_icon:str='', identifier:str='',
    summary:str='', packages:list=<factory>, includes:list=<factory>, excludes:list=<factory>,

    doc_types:list=<factory>, extras:list=<factory>, min_macos:str='11.0',
    category:str='public.app-category.developer-tools'
)->None:
Describe an app once, for whichever freezer this platform uses.


App is the description itself. Only name and entry, the script the app runs, are required; the comment beside each field says what it holds. If you leave out identifier, the reverse-DNS name macOS uses to tell apps apart, it becomes org.<name>.<name> in lower case. bundle_name is the name the freezer gives its output, Demo.app on macOS and Demo elsewhere, and out(root) is where that ends up, under root/dist. The saved output below came from a machine that is not a Mac, so it shows Demo.

app = App(name='Demo', entry='demo_app.py', version='1.2.3', summary='the demo app',
          icon='assets/Demo.icns', packages=['demo', 'fasthtml', 'uvicorn'],
          includes=['demo.cli'], data=data, extras=['desktop'])
app.identifier, app.bundle_name, str(app.out('/build/demo'))

('org.demo.demo', 'Demo', '/build/demo/dist/Demo')



app.info_plist()

{'CFBundleName': 'Demo',
 'CFBundleDisplayName': 'Demo',
 'CFBundleIdentifier': 'org.demo.demo',
 'CFBundleVersion': '1.2.3',
 'CFBundleShortVersionString': '1.2.3',
 'CFBundleGetInfoString': 'the demo app',
 'LSApplicationCategoryType': 'public.app-category.developer-tools',
 'LSMinimumSystemVersion': '11.0',
 'NSHighResolutionCapable': True,

 'NSAppTransportSecurity': {'NSAllowsLocalNetworking': True},
 'LSEnvironment': {'LANG': 'en_US.UTF-8', 'PYTHONUTF8': '1'}}


CFBundleVersion is what Launch Services compares when several copies of one app are registered, so local builds that all carry the same version leave it picking an arbitrary copy. Setting App.build to a value that grows with every build, such as 1.2.3.29600000, makes the newest copy win. CFBundleShortVersionString stays the version, and with no build both entries are the version.

test_eq(App('Demo', 'd.py', version='1.2.3').info_plist()['CFBundleVersion'], '1.2.3')
built = App('Demo', 'd.py', version='1.2.3', build='1.2.3.29600000').info_plist()
test_eq((built['CFBundleVersion'], built['CFBundleShortVersionString']), ('1.2.3.29600000', '1.2.3'))
built['CFBundleVersion']

info_plist returns the entries for Info.plist, the file macOS reads to learn an app’s name, version and abilities. Three of the defaults matter for a web app in a window. NSAllowsLocalNetworking lets the window load pages from the local server over plain HTTP. NSRequiresAquaSystemAppearance set to False lets the app follow dark mode. LSEnvironment sets PYTHONUTF8 and LANG so that Python starts in UTF-8. Any entry in App.plist overrides the default of the same name.

app.py2app_options()['excludes']

['PyQt5',

o = app.py2app_options()
o['packages'].append('scipy')
test_eq(app.packages, ['demo', 'fasthtml', 'uvicorn'])
noisy = App(name='D', entry='e.py', excludes=['mlx', 'mlx', 'tkinter']).excluded('darwin')
test_eq(noisy.count('tkinter'), 1)
test_eq(noisy, sorted(set(noisy)))

title: menus
text:
A host describes its menu bar as data: a list of menus, each with a title and a list of rows. This module defines the row types, and the small part of a keymap a menu needs to read. They are plain dataclasses that do not import pywebview or AppKit, so a host can build and test its menu table on any machine. kavacha.window turns the table into a native menu bar on macOS.

The rows
MenuItem is a row that runs one of the host’s actions, named by action. When the user chooses it, the window calls the host’s on_action with that name. A MenuItem with no action is a separator line, which is why action has a default. kind is either empty or warn. warn marks a row the host may want to draw as destructive, such as one that discards changes; kavacha passes it through without acting on it, and refuses any other value.


source

MenuItem
def MenuItem(
    action:str='', kind:str=''
)->None:
One action in a menu. A blank action is a separator.



MenuItem('open_folder'), MenuItem()

Std is a row that AppKit already knows how to handle, such as Cut, Copy, Paste and Select All, so the host does not handle it at all. The row names an AppKit selector, such as cut:. The menu sends that selector along AppKit’s responder chain, the chain of objects that starts at whatever has keyboard focus, and the first one that understands it acts. key and mods give the row’s shortcut directly, because a row like this has no entry in the host’s keymap.
Js is a row that runs a JavaScript expression in the focused window, for small jobs such as reloading the page that need no action of their own.


source

Std
def Std(
    title:str, selector:str, key:str='', mods:str='mod'
)->None:
A row AppKit handles itself, by sending selector to whatever has focus.

    title:str, expr:str

A row that runs the JavaScript expression expr in the focused window.



Std('Cut', 'cut:', 'x'), Js('Reload', 'location.reload()')



Key bindings
A menu shows each action’s label and shortcut, and the host keeps both in its keymap. kavacha does not read the keymap itself. The host supplies a lookup function that takes an action name and returns a Binding, or None for an action it does not know. A Binding holds the action’s chords, its label, and its scope, meaning where the binding applies. A global binding becomes a menu shortcut. A binding with another scope becomes one only when shared is false, which the host sets when no other scope binds the same chord. A dict’s get method is the simplest lookup, as in the example.


source

Binding
def Binding(
    keys:tuple=(), label:str='', scope:str='global', shared:bool=False
)->None:
What a menu row reads from the host’s keymap: the chords, the label, where it applies, and whether another scope binds its chord.



keys = {'save': Binding(('mod+s',), 'Save'), 'find': Binding(('mod+f',), scope='editor')}
keys.get('save'), keys.get('nothing')

bound is true when the binding has at least one chord. It is worked out from keys instead of being stored, so an unbound action is just Binding() and the two can never disagree.


Chords a menu must not take
A menu shortcut wins over the web page, so a chord the system or a window manager already uses must never become one. RESERVED lists them in the keymap grammar: Hyper (hyper, Command, Control, Option and Shift together) with the keys AeroSpace takes, AeroSpace’s own Control and Option chords, and the macOS system chords. kavacha.window.menu_chord refuses every one of them, and a host can lint its default keymap against the same set.
The launcher’s own rows are Std rows every Mac app has. LAUNCHER_ROWS lists them with their chords, so a host can check that no chord on its own menu bar lands on one of them. Close Window takes ⇧⌘W, which leaves ⌘W for the host’s Close Tab.


How a chord is written for a person
chord_glyph writes one chord the way a Mac menu does: the modifier glyphs in the order ⌃⌥⇧⌘, then the key as a capital letter or a symbol such as ↩︎ or ⌫. With mac=False it writes Ctrl+Shift+P. mod is Command on a Mac and Control elsewhere, hyper is all four modifiers, and a capital letter means Shift. A sequence of chords separated by spaces keeps its spaces. Every place a host shows a chord, such as its menus, palette, help and toasts, can use this one function, so they all agree.

How chord is written for a person: ⌃⌥⇧⌘ and a capital on a Mac, Ctrl+Shift+P elsewhere.

On Linux and Windows, mod is Control. Most chords keep their meaning, but some do not. ⌃⌘F, the Mac chord for Full Screen, becomes Ctrl+F, which is Find. Hide and Minimize have no use under a tiling window manager such as Regolith’s i3 or sway. pc_key gives the chord a Std row takes off a Mac. A Mac-only row takes the chord from a small table: Full Screen is F11, Close Window is Ctrl+Shift+W and Quit is Ctrl+Q. Hide, Hide Others, Minimize, Zoom and Bring All to Front get None, which means that the row is not shown. Every other row keeps its chord, with mod as Control. pc_chord writes any chord in this PC form.
LINUX_RESERVED lists the chords a Linux desktop keeps for itself: Regolith’s and GNOME’s. pc_reserved also refuses every chord with Super, because Regolith owns almost all of them. A host can lint its PC keymap against the same set.
gtk_accel writes a chord as a GTK accelerator, such as <Control><Shift>w. GTK runs a window’s accelerators before the widget that has focus. A native accelerator on Copy would take Ctrl+C away from a terminal in the page, so menu_json gives one only to rows the page never needs. PC_NATIVE names those launcher rows: Quit, Close Window and Full Screen.

A Mac build has requirements that are easy to get wrong: py2app needs a framework build of Python, the bundle should contain the exact package versions in uv.lock, and a build must not overwrite an app that is running. Afterwards you want to know which commit an app came from. check reports on all of this without changing anything, and build does the work.

Create or update the build venv at venv from python, install the project with pinned requirements, and return its Python.


build_venv prepares the environment a macOS build runs in. It creates a virtual environment at venv from the interpreter python, starting again if force is set or if the existing one was made with a different Python version. It installs the pinned requirements from lock_requirements when there are any, installs the project at root in editable mode with its extras, and returns the path of the environment’s Python. build calls it. It has no example here because it installs packages.

Return the commit, dirty flag, version and build time for the checkout at root, or None outside one.


A bundle is a copy of your code, and nothing in it says which version of the source it came from. A stamp records that. It is a small JSON file named build.json (the name is in STAMP) that holds the git commit, whether the checkout had uncommitted changes, the version and the build time.
stamp_path says where the stamp goes: inside Contents/Resources for a .app, and next to the executable for anything else. It decides by the .app suffix alone, so it works for a bundle that has not been built yet.

stamp_path('/dist/Demo.app'), stamp_path('/dist/Demo')

(Path('/dist/Demo.app/Contents/Resources/build.json'),
 Path('/dist/Demo/build.json'))


git_stamp collects the stamp’s fields from the git checkout at root, or returns None if root is not in one. write_stamp writes the stamp into a bundle and returns it. Outside a checkout the commit is left empty, and if the bundle’s folder does not exist nothing is written. read_stamp reads the stamp back, and returns None if the bundle has none or it cannot be parsed.

st = write_stamp(repo/'dist'/'Demo.app', repo, version='2.0.1')
st['commit'][:12], st['dirty'], st['version']

('3b2bbb3a952a', False, '2.0.1')



read_stamp(repo/'dist'/'Demo.app') == st

True


If tracked files have changes that are not committed, the stamp says dirty, and build prints that next to the commit. When an app misbehaves, you can then tell whether it was built from code that was never committed.

def build(
    spec, root, setup_py, venv:NoneType=None, alias:bool=False, force:bool=False, rebuild_venv:bool=False,
    identity:NoneType=None
):
Freeze spec into root/dist, switching to a framework Python first on macOS when needed.


build freezes spec into root/dist and returns the path of the result. setup_py is the script that calls the freezer for your app. It will not start while a copy of the app is running, unless you pass force=True, because the build replaces the standard library the running app imports from, and that app then fails with a zip error that says nothing about the build.
On macOS it next checks the interpreter. If the current Python is not a framework build, build finds one with framework_python, prepares an environment with build_venv (pass rebuild_venv=True to make it from scratch), runs the script that called build again with that environment’s Python, and returns. The environment variable KAVACHA_BUILD_VENV (the name is in REEXEC) marks the second run, so a Python that is still unsuitable stops the build instead of looping.
On a framework Python, and on Windows, it runs the freezer, calls finish on macOS with identity, writes the stamp, and prints where the app is and which commit it was built from. alias=True asks py2app for an alias build, which refers to your source files instead of copying them and is quicker while you develop.

title: thin
text:
A thin app is a small native launcher. It owns the windows, and it runs the app’s Python server as its child. The Python packages do not ship in the app: they come from a signed environment lock that has its own number and its own channel. contract/api-1.md in this repository gives the contract between the launcher, the server and the lock tools.
This module describes one thin app with Thin. Every name the launcher, the lock tools and the server use comes from it: the support folder, the env marker, the signing namespace, the <PREFIX>_* variables, the bridge handler. Thin.config writes kavacha.json, which the launcher reads in place of constants. Thin.info_plist writes the bundle’s Info.plist, and childenv gives the clean child environment.

The child environment
CHILDENV is the environment spec that the launcher and the lock tools both read. The common keys apply to every OS; a key under darwin, linux or win32 replaces the common one on that OS. {prefix} is the app’s variable prefix, such as LEELA_.
childenv flattens the spec for one OS and fills in the prefix. The launcher’s bundle holds the flat form, so the Swift and Rust sides read one shape.

s = childenv('LEELA_', 'darwin')
test_eq(s['drop_prefixes'], ['UV_', 'LEELA_HOST_', 'LEELA_LOCK_', 'LEELA_ENV_', 'LEELA_APP_'])

w = childenv('X_', 'win32')
test_eq((w['uv']['UV_LINK_MODE'], w['uv']['UV_NO_CONFIG']), ('copy', '1'))



The spec
Thin is a flat dataclass. A field left empty is derived from name, so an app gives only what differs. The groups are: identity, the server, lock signing, the lock, the native capabilities and the distribution.

def Thin(
    name:str, identifier:str='', package:str='', version:str='0.0.0', build:str='', summary:str='', copyright:str='',
    category:str='public.app-category.developer-tools', repo:str='', server:str='', server_args:list=<factory>,
    health:str='/health', env_prefix:str='', api:int=1, sig_ns:str='', marker:str='',
    keys:str='packaging/lock/keys.pub', key_names:list=<factory>, lock_dir:str='packaging/lock', lock_project:str='',
    python:str='3.13.18', platforms:list=<factory>, macos_min:str='14.0', extras:list=<factory>, seed_extra:str='',
    owners:list=<factory>, owner_org:str='', wheels:dict=<factory>, source_only:list=<factory>,
    imports:list=<factory>, cooldown:int=7, record_days:int=7, hooks:str='', childenv:str='',
    uv_version:str='packaging/uv.version', build_dir:str='build/thin', uv_sha256:str='packaging/uv.sha256',
    bridge:list=<factory>, bridge_global:str='pywebview', sites:dict=<factory>, routes:dict=<factory>,
    capabilities:list=<factory>, menus:str='/app/menu.json', menu_action_js:str='leeAct({action})',
    window:dict=<factory>, titlebar:str='native', doc_types:list=<factory>, imported_types:list=<factory>,
    url_schemes:list=<factory>, usage:dict=<factory>, entitlements:dict=<factory>, icon:str='', cask:str='',
    cask_template:str='', tap:str='', homepage:str='', winget:str='', launcher:str='', launcher_sha256:str='',
    max_mb:int=60, max_zip_mb:int=25
)->None:
One thin app: identity, server, lock signing, lock, native capabilities and distribution.


Thin.load reads the spec from [tool.kavacha.thin] in pyproject.toml, or from packaging/kavacha.toml. A TOML table such as [lock] only groups its keys: lock.python is the field python. A table whose name is also a field, such as [sites], stays a table.

import tempfile
d = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(d/'packaging').mkdir(); (d/'packaging'/'kavacha.toml').write_text('name = "Demo"\nrepo = "me/demo"\n[lock]\npython = "3.12.9"\nextras = ["a", "b"]\n[sites]\nlist = "/s"\n')
t = Thin.load(d)
test_eq((t.python, t.extras, t.sites, t.seed_extra), ('3.12.9', ['a', 'b'], {'list': '/s'}, 'b'))
test_eq((t.identifier, t.sig_ns, t.marker, t.env_prefix, t.cask, t.owner_org), ('org.demo.demo', 'demo-lock', '.demo-env.json', 'DEMO_', 'demo', 'me'))



What the launcher reads
Thin.config is kavacha.json, the launcher’s only source of names. A launcher that finds no such file, or one with a higher api than its own, refuses to start.
Thin.info_plist is the bundle’s Info.plist. The launcher binary is always MacOS/<name>, and the icon is Resources/AppIcon.icns.

t = Thin('Demo', version='1.0.0', build='4', url_schemes=['demo'], usage={'NSMicrophoneUsageDescription': 'to listen'})
p = t.info_plist()
test_eq((p['CFBundleExecutable'], p['CFBundleVersion'], p['CFBundleURLTypes'][0]['CFBundleURLSchemes']), ('Demo', '4', ['demo']))
test_eq(p['NSMicrophoneUsageDescription'], 'to listen')
c = t.config()
test_eq((c['support'], c['bridge']['handler'], c['bridge']['flag'], c['debug_env'], c['python']), ('Demo', 'demo', '__demo', 'DEMO_WEBVIEW_DEBUG', '3.13'))

Thin.spec_env is the flat child environment for this app: the app’s own JSON file when it gives one, else kavacha’s with its prefix and server arguments.

test_eq(Thin('Demo', server_args=['--app', '--port', '{port}']).spec_env('darwin')['server_args'], ['--app', '--port', '{port}'])

Thin.write puts the three generated files in a folder: kavacha.json, childenv.json and Info.plist.

o = Thin('Demo').write(Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()))
test_eq(sorted(f.name for f in o.iterdir()), ['Info.plist', 'childenv.json', 'kavacha.json'])



The command line
kavacha lock … is the lock tool (kavacha.lock), and kavacha ship mac … builds and ships the app (kavacha.ship).
